newsitem.title: JAPAN: LTCB-Swiss Bank deal may spur Japan bank alliances.
newsitem.headline: LTCB-Swiss Bank deal may spur Japan bank alliances.

text.p: The surprise announcement of an alliance between the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan Ltd (LTCB) and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) may spur other big Japanese banks to quick action on new strategies, including alliances with foreign banks, analysts said on Wednesday.
Japan's "Big Bang" financial reforms are expected to shrink business in ordinary banking services while boosting demand for securities and asset management services, they said.

They added that, to deal with this changing environment, Japan's big banks must quickly decide which direction to pursue: teaming up with Western partners, or forming holding companies with domestic financial firms.

"Looking at the alliance between LTCB and SBC, Japanese banks began to fear that they may lose potentially good Western partners if they don't take action now," said Yushiro Ikuyo, first vice president of Smith Barney International.

He said that big Japanese banks, many of which will finally cut their problem loans to manageable levels within a year or so, must seek potential Western partners experienced in investment products that can lure new customers, as they strive to maintain their presence in global markets.

Western banks, which have yet to cultivate Japan's cash-rich markets effectively, are keen to tie up with domestic banks so they can make the best use of their innovative financial skills and expand in the markets, he added.

On Tuesday, LTCB and SBC said they agreed to form a strategic alliance that includes cross-shareholdings of three percent. The banks will set up three joint firms based in Japan to cover investment banking, asset management and private banking.

Akira Takai, an analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research, said Western banks are not interested in retail banking services in Japan but are eager to grab shares of the lucrative securities and asset management businesses.
Trust banks and Daiwa Bank Ltd are allowed to engage in both ordinary banking and the management of investors' funds.

Analysts said, however, that Japan's top six commercial banks and the Industrial Bank of Japan (IBJ) are likely to opt for setting up financial conglomerates with domestic firms instead of foreign alliances.

Yoshinobu Yamada, an analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc, said that if there is a large gap in the size of assets at a commercial bank and a trust bank in the same corporate group, and if their customer base is different, they are likely to choose to convert to a holding-company structure.
Japan will end a ban on banks forming financial holding firms, probably in 1998, under reforms that will eliminate barriers between banks, brokerages and insurers.

Japan's six biggest banks -- Sumitomo Bank Ltd, Sakura Bank Ltd, Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd, Fuji Bank Ltd, Sanwa Bank Ltd and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank -- all lead major corporate groups that maintain cross-shareholdings and long-term business ties.
Some analysts said that a holding company combining Fuji Bank and financially weak Yasuda Trust & Banking Co Ltd was relatively likely, as the two banks are in the same Fuyo corporate group.

While Japan's biggest trust bank, Mitsubishi Trust & Banking Corp, is in the same group as the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, their corporate cultures are so different that it would be unlikely for them to form a holding company, analysts said.
The same is also true of Sumitomo Trust & Banking Co Ltd, Japan's second biggest trust bank, and Sumitomo Bank, they said.
